nonObvious.text: A cafe runs out of bar, not out of customers: at 200 orders a day the 8am hour alone brings 28 to 36 orders, and one barista makes about 25.
nonObvious.why: Monthly capacity looks fine on paper while the shop turns people away every morning and stands idle every afternoon. The fix is the schedule, not headcount.

nonObvious.text: People judge a line by how long it looks, not by how fast it moves.
nonObvious.why: A fast bar with eight people in the doorway loses more walk-ins than a slow one with three. Where the line stands and how it is seen from the street matter as much as speed.

nonObvious.text: Phone orders can lose you walk-in customers.
nonObvious.why: When a fifth of rush orders came by phone, Starbucks found people saw the crowd at the handoff and left without ordering. Order-ahead needs a cap in the rush.

nonObvious.text: A star on Yelp is worth 5-9% of revenue to an independent and nothing to a chain.
nonObvious.why: People already know what a chain is. Reviews are how a stranger decides about you, so they matter most on tourist streets and least among regulars.

nonObvious.text: A 4.24 and a 4.26 are the same cafe, but one shows four stars and the other four and a half.
nonObvious.why: Ratings are rounded to half stars, and the jump at the rounding line changed how often restaurants sold out by 19 percentage points.

nonObvious.text: A quarter of your Yelp reviews may never count, and the ones you asked for are the first to go.
nonObvious.why: Yelp says about 75% of reviews are 'recommended'; the rest are hidden from the rating. Reviews from first-time reviewers and solicited reviews are filtered most.

nonObvious.text: A free cookie for a five-star review is a federal violation.
nonObvious.why: The FTC's 2024 review rule bans rewards that depend on what the review says, with penalties up to $53,088 per violation. Asking everyone for an honest review is legal.

nonObvious.text: Answering reviews raises the rating.
nonObvious.why: Hotels that began replying gained 0.12 stars, and a third of them moved up a displayed half star within six months. Future reviewers write more carefully when they see the owner reads.

nonObvious.text: With a B at re-inspection you may post 'Grade Pending' and argue your case; you may not leave the window empty.
nonObvious.why: The pending card is legal until the hearing and reads better than a B. A missing card is a separate fine and an easy 311 complaint for a neighbor.

nonObvious.text: An office-district cafe earns its week in three days.
nonObvious.why: Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday hold 70% of weekday office visits; Friday holds 12%, and 11.9% in New York. Rent is paid for seven days.

nonObvious.text: For a neighborhood cafe Saturday is the best day and Monday the worst.
nonObvious.why: Cafes and bakeries sell 15% above their weekly average on Saturday and about 10% below it on Monday: the opposite of an office block. The same staffing plan cannot serve both.

nonObvious.text: The city's weekends recovered; its weekdays did not.
nonObvious.why: Weekend subway ridership is at 89% of 2019, weekday ridership at 74%. A lease priced on pre-pandemic weekday crowds is priced on people who are not there.

nonObvious.text: August is the national peak for eating out and a slow month in New York.
nonObvious.why: Residents leave, offices thin out from late July to Labor Day and students are gone. Tourist streets are the exception.

nonObvious.text: The worst office weeks are not in summer: they run from Thanksgiving into January.
nonObvious.why: Office visits in December 2025 were 33% under 2019, against 22% under in July. A commuter-fed cafe should plan its cash for a weak December and January, not only for August.

nonObvious.text: A delivery app's 15% is not the whole bill.
nonObvious.why: New York caps delivery at 15%, basic service at 5% and card processing at 3%: 23% together. Since 2025 an app may sell 'enhanced' services for up to 20% more. On a small coffee ticket the promoted plan leaves under 30 cents of contribution per dollar.

nonObvious.text: If an app overcharged you, the city can get the money back.
nonObvious.why: In April 2026 the consumer agency won more than $580,000 in refunds for over 380 restaurants from one delivery app that broke the fee caps.

nonObvious.text: Higher courier pay did not shrink delivery in New York.
nonObvious.why: The city forecast fewer orders when it set the courier minimum. Orders rose instead: 3.3 million a week in mid-2026, 700,000 more than in December 2023.

nonObvious.text: You cannot add a card fee at the register, but you can post two prices.
nonObvious.why: State law requires the posted price to be the full credit card price, and the city bars restaurants from adding surcharge lines. A cash price next to a card price is the lawful form, and it still costs customers: most people switch payment or shop to avoid it.

nonObvious.text: A chain opening next door hurts the afternoon more than the morning, and it can be answered.
nonObvious.why: One owner lost a tenth of afternoon sales to a new Starbucks and won them back by adding breakfast sandwiches. Between near-identical stores the measured effect is about 1% per neighbor.

nonObvious.text: Chains are leaving New York faster than they arrive.
nonObvious.why: Chain stores fell in six of the last eight years; Starbucks closed 42 city stores in 2025. Each closure releases a few hundred daily customers to whoever is nearest and fast enough.

nonObvious.text: The new rival is not Starbucks: it is an app with $1.99 coffee and a 500-square-foot counter.
nonObvious.why: An app-first chain went from 2 to 22 New York stores in about a year, and a small-format chain with automatic machines reached 106 stores. Both sell the commuter's cup cheaper than a full cafe can.

nonObvious.text: The city is licensing thousands more food carts, and a coffee cart needs no rent.
nonObvious.why: 2,200 more vendor licenses a year from 2026 to 2031. A cart at the subway stairs sells coffee for about $2, where your commuters pass first.

nonObvious.text: Regulars are a few hundred people who pay most of the rent.
nonObvious.why: A regular brings six times the yearly revenue of a one-time customer; at one roastery two thirds of revenue came from repeat customers. Losing one barista they like can cost more than a bad review.

nonObvious.text: Most first-time customers do not come back.
nonObvious.why: Between a fifth and two thirds of first visitors are gone within 100 days. The opening crowd is not the customer base; the second visit is what must be earned.

nonObvious.text: Closing at 3pm can be the right decision.
nonObvious.why: The last four hours carry about a quarter of a neighborhood cafe's orders and a full crew's wages. Below about 100 orders a day the afternoon loses money.

nonObvious.text: An 'unlimited' coffee pass will be capped sooner or later.
nonObvious.why: The best-known subscription ran four years as unlimited and then limited holders to 30 drinks a month: the heaviest users drink the margin.

nonObvious.text: A dog-friendly cafe is illegal indoors in New York.
nonObvious.why: Only service dogs may enter a food establishment; pet dogs are allowed in outdoor seating with a posted sign. A dog inside is a Health Department violation and counts toward the letter grade.

nonObvious.text: Flyers are fined per flyer.
nonObvious.why: Each one taped to a pole or tucked under a wiper is a separate violation of $75 to $250, and the fine goes to the business named on it. Handing flyers to people is legal.

nonObvious.text: Prices on the street rise about 4% a year, so standing still is a price cut.
nonObvious.why: Median drip coffee rose 4.3% and cold brew 4.0% in a year. Customers accept small regular steps; they notice a jump.

nonObvious.text: When the chain down the street closed its restrooms to non-customers, the requests moved to its neighbors.
nonObvious.why: Starbucks ended its open-door policy in January 2025. A cafe with fewer than 20 seats has no duty to offer a restroom at all, and saying yes has a cleaning cost.

nonObvious.text: Taste, not price, is what people say makes them pick one coffee shop over another.
nonObvious.why: In a 2025 survey of 650 coffee drinkers 53% named taste, 20% price, 17% convenience and 8% atmosphere. What they say and what they do differ, but it is a reason not to compete on price alone.

nonObvious.text: Going viral is a capacity problem.
nonObvious.why: A Brooklyn cafe had to cut its line off at 3pm; a Manhattan luncheonette had two-to-three-hour waits for months and 'wasn't ready'. The surge leaves reviews behind, good or bad, long after the crowd is gone.

nonObvious.text: In New York a coffee cart charges about $2, a chain about $3 and a specialty bar $6 to $8 for a milk drink.
nonObvious.why: Three price worlds share one sidewalk. A cafe that prices like a specialty bar and serves like a chain is compared with the cheaper one.

nonObvious.text: Evenings belong to a different kind of cafe.
nonObvious.why: Late-night coffee is growing where coffee, not alcohol, is the social drink: Yemeni-style cafes stay open late across North America, and some New York shops turn into wine or sake bars after dark. An ordinary espresso bar that simply stays open later rarely covers the payroll.

No official count was read; the Health Department grades about 27,000-29,000 restaurants of all kinds.
